summary: Background: The Functional Independence Measure (FIM) is a standard functional assessment tool in rehabilitation medicine; however, formal assessments are often conducted only at limited intervals. Free-text clinical notes contain more frequent observations of patients’ functional status and may complement these assessments. Objective: This study aimed to estimate item-level FIM scores from Japanese free-text rehabilitation notes using a locally deployed large language model (LLM) and to evaluate estimation performance; item-level estimability; and differences across diseases, therapy types, and admission FIM severity groups. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed free-text notes from physical therapy (PT), occupational therapy (OT), and speech-language pathology (SLP) for patients hospitalized with cerebral infarction (CeI), hip fracture (HF), or vertebral fracture (VBF) at Saiseikai Moriyama Municipal Hospital between October 2019 and September 2024. Using zero-shot prompting, an LLM estimated all FIM items from each note. Estimated scores were matched to reference FIM scores recorded for the same patient on the same calendar date. Performance was evaluated using the mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error, and quadratic weighted kappa. Estimation rates and comparisons with modal-score and last-observation-carried-forward (LOCF) baselines were also examined. Results: Among 2,952,702 eligible note-item pairs from 164,039 retained rehabilitation-note-level outputs, the model produced 980,000 valid estimates, corresponding to an overall estimation rate of 33.2%. Among 170,744 note-item opportunities with an available same-day reference score, 57,246 (33.5%) were estimable, of which 77.7% (44,481/57,246) were within 1 point of the reference score. Estimates derived from OT notes had a lower MAE than those derived from PT notes in CeI and HF, whereas the difference was not significant in VBF. The LLM outperformed the modal-score baseline but had a higher MAE than the LOCF overall (0.825 vs 0.648). Conclusions: The locally deployed LLM shows the potential to derive item-level FIM estimates from Japanese rehabilitation notes. Among estimable note-item pairs with a same-day reference FIM score, 77.7% were within 1 point of the reference score. These findings support the potential use of LLM-based estimation to structure functional information contained in routine rehabilitation notes and complement periodic FIM assessments. Further integration of multidisciplinary clinical records and external validation are needed to improve estimability and evaluate its value for longitudinal functional monitoring.
title: Estimating Functional Independence Measure Scores From Japanese Rehabilitation Notes Using a Large Language Model: Retrospective Study

summary: Ambient AI scribes have been rapidly adopted across health care organizations to mitigate documentation burden and burnout. Initial single-system reports described substantial time savings, but more recent multisite evaluations and meta-analyses describe modest, heterogeneous effects with generally low methodological quality. Most evaluations emphasize efficiency and satisfaction, leaving potential effects on communication quality, narrative preservation, cognitive performance, and equity largely unmeasured. This viewpoint aimed to characterize evaluation patterns in prominent ambient AI scribe implementations, explain why unmeasured domains warrant investigation for patient safety and care quality, and propose an expanded framework with feasible research priorities. This analytic viewpoint mapped evaluation domain coverage in a purposive, illustrative sample of prominent implementation reports published through April 2026, then synthesized findings with literature on clinical communication, narrative medicine, automation effects, and health equity. Reporting was guided by Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) principles for narrative reviews; PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) was not used because the work is a domain-coverage characterization rather than an evidence synthesis estimating effects. A single reviewer (VSME) performed selection and extraction, consistent with the viewpoint’s illustrative intent. Across the included implementations, evaluation consistently measured documentation time, after-hours work, and clinician satisfaction. Within this illustrative sample of 6 independently peer-reviewed real-world implementation evaluations, we did not identify any that reported systematic assessment of patient-clinician communication using validated instruments, structured comparison of AI-generated against human-generated notes for narrative fidelity, longitudinal evaluation of cognitive or educational effects, or equity analyses stratified by language and demographic group. The absence in this purposive sample reflects an absence of public reporting rather than proof that no organization has measured these dimensions internally. Limited error analyses found frequent omissions, with accuracy declining as encounter complexity increased. Evidence from multilingual and interpreter-mediated encounters was notably sparse. Current evidence supports continued implementation with quality safeguards in settings where benefits are demonstrated locally rather than universal adoption on the strength of early single-system reports. Organizations implementing ambient AI scribes should consider embedding prospective evaluation across 4 domains: validated communication quality measurement, structured narrative content comparison, longitudinal cognitive and training studies, and equity analyses across languages and demographics. Three near-term priorities offer immediate feasibility for organizations with evaluation capacity: (1) deploying validated communication instruments such as the Communication Assessment Tool or Consumer Assessment of Health Care Providers and Systems (CAHPS) within ongoing rollouts; (2) launching multisite longitudinal trainee cohorts comparing programs with and without ambient AI exposure; and (3) oversampling multilingual and interpreter-mediated encounters for stratified equity analyses. Narrative preservation requires foundational methodological work before implementation-ready measures exist. Editors, implementers, and vendors can each act now: editors by requiring domain-coverage reporting; implementers by preregistering evaluation plans before rollout; vendors by publishing stratified performance data as a routine condition of deployment. The goal is to preserve documented efficiency gains while generating evidence about communication, narrative, reasoning, and equity dimensions that current evaluations leave unmeasured.
title: Beyond Time Saved: A Framework for Comprehensive Evaluation of AI Clinical Documentation

summary: Background: Publicly accessible, internet-based AI chatbots have emerged as unregulated digital health resources that clinicians and patients consult in real time, including during acute medical emergencies. In dental practice—where life-threatening events such as anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest, and severe hypoglycemia can unfold within seconds—the unsupervised use of these tools as point-of-care decision aids poses uncharacterized patient safety risks. Despite widespread deployment, no study has systematically evaluated the accuracy, temporal consistency, or multilingual reliability of contemporary large language model (LLM)–based chatbots specifically for dental medical emergency management. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the accuracy, temporal stability, and multilingual performance of five contemporary LLM-based chatbots when queried on the management of medical emergencies in dental practice. Methods: A comparative study was conducted to assess five AI chatbots: ChatGPT-5.2 (OpenAI), Gemini 3.1 (Google), DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek AI), Grok 4.20 (xAI), and Kimi K2.5 (Moonshot AI). A total of 130 questions covering dental medical emergency management were developed and categorized into four formats: multiple-choice questions (MCQs), yes-or-no questions, open-ended WH questions, and clinical scenario questions. Each question was presented using two prompting strategies (basic and advanced) across three languages (English, Arabic, and Chinese). Data collection was performed over seven consecutive days, generating 27,300 chatbot responses. Responses were evaluated by language-specific expert reviewers and classified as correct or incorrect based on established clinical references. Statistical analysis was performed using chi-square tests to assess associations between accuracy and study variables. Pairwise post hoc comparisons of column proportions were conducted using z-tests with Bonferroni correction. Results: A total of 27,300 responses were analyzed; 25,377 (92.96%) were correct. Question type significantly influenced chatbot performance (<.001), with MCQs demonstrating the highest accuracy (5942/6300, 94.3%), and WH questions demonstrating the lowest accuracy (7686/8400, 91.5%). Language also showed a significant association with accuracy (=.01), with English prompts achieving the highest accuracy (8512/9100, 93.5%). Chatbot model performance differed significantly (<.001), with Gemini 3.1 demonstrating the highest accuracy (5176/5460, 94.8%; 95% CI 94.21%‐95.39%), followed by ChatGPT-5.2 (5105/5460, 93.5%; 95% CI 92.85%‐94.15%) and Kimi K2.5 (5071/5460, 92.9%). Prompt complexity and testing day did not significantly affect response accuracy (=.69 and =.96, respectively). Conclusions: Current LLM-based chatbots demonstrate high accuracy in answering structured questions related to dental medical emergency management. However, performance varies according to question format and language, and the presence of incorrect responses highlights potential safety concerns. AI chatbots may serve as educational tools, but their use as real-time decision support during dental medical emergencies should be approached with caution.
title: Evaluating Internet-Based AI Chatbots as Unregulated Digital Health Resources in Dental Emergency Management: Comparative Multilingual Study

summary: Background: With the rapid expansion of health care data, multiple international standardized terminology systems have been developed and refined to ensure semantic interoperability, which is a crucial factor in facilitating collaborative use. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the real-world use and applicability of standardized terminology systems by mapping clinical terms from routine cancer care and to propose guidelines that optimize mapping. Methods: Clinical terms generated during cancer care at the National Cancer Center Korea were extracted and mapped to multiple target terminology systems: the Korean Standard Classification of Diseases; ; Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes; RxNorm; Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classification; and Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine Clinical Terms (SNOMED CT). A multidisciplinary working group of health care information managers, data experts, and oncologists verified the mapping outcomes, calculated the cross-verification discordance rate, and compared the coverage across systems. Results: A total of 3472 source terms were identified across 7 domains: chief complaint, diagnosis, laboratory test, imaging test, surgery/procedure, medication, and radiation therapy. With postcoordination and predefined mapping guidelines, SNOMED CT achieved high overall mapping rates (98.3%‐100%) across domains. Applying postcoordination as needed substantially improved exact semantic match rates, which exceeded 90% in most domains. However, more than 40% of source terms were broadly mapped in the imaging test and radiation therapy domains because procedural details such as imaging technique and radiation field configuration could not be represented in SNOMED CT. The cross-verification discordance rate between mappers, defined as the proportion of source terms with disagreement, remained low (0.3%‐1.3%). RxNorm and Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes showed complementary strengths within their specialized domains, adding detail or specificity where SNOMED CT was less complete. Conclusions: Standardized terminology systems are feasible and effective in encoding clinical terms for cancer care. SNOMED CT was the most comprehensive, and predefined mapping guidelines provide a structured framework for mapping and consensus resolution. Domain-specific systems should be used alongside SNOMED CT, and all systems should be updated regularly to reflect evolving clinical practice.
title: Real-World Applicability of Multiple International Terminology Systems in Oncology: Mapping Study of Clinical Terms for Cancer Diagnosis and Treatment

summary: Background: Early-stage pulmonary sarcoidosis with serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (sACE) activity within the normal range is difficult to distinguish from other pulmonary diseases with similar radiographic characteristics. Objective: This study aimed to develop and validate machine learning (ML)–based diagnostic models for differentiating early-stage pulmonary sarcoidosis using indices from routine peripheral blood tests. Methods: From May 2014 to May 2021, a total of 1142 patients with atypical initial pulmonary imaging findings were enrolled. After applying strict inclusion and exclusion criteria, 420 cases were divided into sarcoidosis and nonsarcoidosis groups (including mediastinal lymph node tuberculosis [MLNT], lung cancer, lymphoma, and pneumoconiosis), then stratified by sex and randomly split (7:3) into training and validation sets. Features were selected via univariate analysis (P<.10), the Boruta algorithm, and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression. Six ML algorithms—logistic regression (LR), random forest, support vector machine (SVM), extreme gradient boosting, k‑nearest neighbor, and naïve Bayes—were compared using area under the curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1-score, Brier score, calibration assessment, and decision curve analysis. Shapley Additive Explanations was used for interpretability. The selected models were deployed as an interactive Shiny web application. Results: After stratification, the male group comprised 224 cases (sarcoidosis n=42; MLNT: n=39; lung cancer: n=106; lymphoma: n=9; pneumoconiosis: n=28), and the female group comprised 196 cases (sarcoidosis: n=100; MLNT: n=39; lung cancer: n=49; lymphoma: n=4; pneumoconiosis: n=4). Models were selected based on comprehensive evaluation of multiple performance metrics, including AUC, accuracy, specificity, F1-score, and Brier score. The selected model for the male group was SVM, incorporating the following indices: age, lymphocyte count (Lym#), red cell distribution width standard deviation, D-dimer, sACE, cluster of differentiation 4-positive T cells to cluster of differentiation 8-positive T cells ratio (CD4+/CD8+), erythrocyte sedimentation rate, triglyceride to high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio (TG/HDLC), basophil count, and total protein. The selected model for the female group was LR, using Lym#, sACE, total cholesterol, TG/HDLC, glucose, CD3+%, and CD8+%. The validation set results showed AUCs of 0.896 (95% CI 0.746-1.000) and 0.762 (95% CI 0.632-0.892), sensitivities of 0.700 (95% CI 0.397-0.892) and 0.679 (95% CI 0.493-0.821), and specificities of 0.942 (95% CI 0.844-0.980) and 0.815 (95% CI 0.633-0.918), respectively. Conclusions: Based on sex‑stratified strategies, the models demonstrated preliminary discriminative ability for differentiating early‑stage pulmonary sarcoidosis with normal sACE from other pulmonary diseases. However, the wide CIs preclude definitive conclusions about clinical performance, and external validation in larger cohorts is needed.
title: Differential Diagnosis of Early-Stage Pulmonary Sarcoidosis With Normal Serum Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Activity Using Peripheral Blood Indicators: Machine Learning Models Development and Validation

summary: Background: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common, life-threatening complication among hospitalized patients. Timely prediction is crucial for prevention, while accurate prognosis following onset is essential for guiding care. Although electronic health records (EHRs) provide rich longitudinal data, their high dimensionality, heterogeneity, and temporal complexity pose challenges for traditional machine learning. Objective: The aim of this study was to develop and evaluate a transformer-based model for generalizable AKI prediction and prognosis by modeling long-range temporal dependencies and complex relationships in heterogeneous EHR data and to examine its interpretability. Methods: We developed the Biomarker-Aware Transformer for AKI (BAT-AKI), which integrates multidimensional embeddings capturing temporal dynamics, textual descriptions, hierarchical ontology structures, and semantic relationships in EHRs. To enhance sensitivity to AKI-related biomarker fluctuations, BAT-AKI combines masked language modeling with a novel biomarker abnormality-aware pretraining task. The model was pretrained and fine-tuned for 4 tasks: AKI onset, early reversal, recovery at discharge, and 90-day post-AKI mortality. Pretraining and internal validation used data from the National Patient-Centered Clinical Research Network (PCORnet) site, with external validation across 3 additional sites. Results: BAT-AKI achieved the strongest overall discrimination, outperforming baseline models in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) on most tasks. For AKI onset prediction, it achieved an AUROC of 0.8549 (95% CI 0.8433-0.8658) and an AUPRC of 0.6041 (95% CI 0.5786-0.6292), exceeding the second-best baseline by 2.8% in AUROC and 8.1% in AUPRC. Across prognostic tasks, BAT-AKI achieved AUROCs of 0.6006 (95% CI 0.5703-0.6318), 0.6080 (95% CI 0.5745-0.6397), and 0.8017 (95% CI 0.7708-0.8311) and AUPRCs of 0.7036 (95% CI 0.6690-0.7388), 0.7417 (95% CI 0.7082-0.7765), and 0.5063 (95% CI 0.4422-0.5684) for early reversal, recovery at discharge, and 90-day post-AKI mortality, respectively, corresponding to relative gains of 2.4% to 6% in AUROC and 3.7% to 4.1% in AUPRC over the second-best baseline. Performance remained stable across external cohorts, with AKI onset AUROCs ranging from 0.7754 (95% CI 0.7677-0.7827) to 0.7989 (95% CI 0.7885-0.8092) and AUPRCs ranging from 0.4777 (95% CI 0.4631-0.4924) to 0.5687 (95% CI 0.5495-0.5871), corresponding to relative improvements of 3.7% to 5.3% in AUROC and 16.8% to 25.3% in AUPRC over the transformer baseline. In a low-resource setting using only 2% of the fine-tuning data, BAT-AKI achieved an AUROC of 0.7898 (95% CI 0.7759-0.8036) and an AUPRC of 0.4903 (95% CI 0.4640-0.5178) for AKI onset prediction, exceeding the second-best baseline by 4.2% in AUROC and 10.9% in AUPRC. Visualization of embeddings, attention patterns, and integrated-gradient feature attributions highlighted clinically meaningful relationships and patient-specific trajectories. Conclusions: BAT-AKI provides generalizable AKI prediction and prognosis with consistent discrimination across institutions, while offering interpretability insights into its predictions, supporting its potential for early warning and AKI care optimization. title: Early Prediction and Prognosis in Acute Kidney Injury Using a Biomarker-Aware Transformer: Retrospective Multicenter Study

summary: Background: Anxiety problems are prevalent among autistic children and adolescents and those with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Natural language processing (NLP) is increasingly used to structure information from electronic health records (EHRs), but its implementation within secure child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS) research environments is less frequently reported. Objective: This study documented the specification, governance, integration, and evaluation of an NLP-enabled information extraction workflow within the Oxford Health National Health Service (NHS) Foundation Trust CAMHS research setting for extracting documented anxiety treatment information and outcome-related text from the EHRs of autistic young people and those with ADHD and examined implementation using normalization process theory (NPT). Methods: A multidisciplinary team developed a locally deployed NLP pipeline to identify labeled text spans describing presenting problems, medication attributes, psychological therapies, and treatment outcomes in pseudonymized EHR notes. Implementation followed an iterative seven-phase road map: (1) defining research questions, (2) identifying key constructs, (3) codeveloping an annotation schema, (4) training human annotators, (5) resolving annotation discrepancies, (6) large-scale annotation of EHR data, and (7) developing and evaluating the NLP model. NPT was applied throughout to guide implementation and evaluate progress. Quantitative outcomes (data volume processed, annotation reliability, and model performance) and qualitative feedback were collected to assess implementation success. Results: The source cohort comprised 454,127 notes from 5906 patients; 697 (0.2%) randomly selected, manually annotated notes from 302 (5.1%) patients were used for model development and held-out evaluation. Category-specific position-based Krippendorff α values ranged from 0.325 to 0.579 for problem, psychological therapy, and outcome spans and from 0.665 to 0.967 for medication spans. Agreement was highest for medication names, doses, and frequencies and lowest for cognitive problems and treatment outcomes. Held-out macroaveraged F1-score was 0.87 (95% CI 0.86-0.89) across the 4 medication labels and 0.71 (95% CI 0.68-0.73) across the 5 problem labels, psychological therapy labels, and outcome labels; label-specific F1-score ranged from 0.60 to 0.98. Team-generated implementation records indicated that multidisciplinary schema development and clear protocols supported shared understanding and engagement, whereas annotation burden, documentation variability, data access delays, and computing constraints impeded implementation. No major adverse events or harms were reported. Conclusions: This report demonstrates the feasibility of integrating NLP tools into NHS CAMHS research workflows to extract structured information on anxiety treatments from routine clinical records. The NPT framework provided a structured approach for documenting the organizational work, barriers, and adaptations involved. External validation, refinement of less reliable labels, and further evaluation are required before broader use.
title: Integrating Natural Language Processing in Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services Research Using Normalization Process Theory: Implementation Report

summary: Background: Major adverse renal and cardiovascular events (MARCE) have been proposed as a comprehensive end point reflecting both cardiac and renal outcomes in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) and chronic kidney disease (CKD). However, existing prediction tools lack accuracy and generalizability for this high-risk population. Objective: This study aimed to develop and externally validate explainable machine learning models and a nomogram for predicting in-hospital MARCE among patients with AMI and CKD. Methods: We enrolled patients with AMI and CKD who underwent emergency treatment at the First Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University as the discovery cohort and those at Wenzhou TCM (traditional Chinese medicine) Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University as the external validation cohort. Clinical features, including demographic details, comorbidities, laboratory results, echocardiography measurements, procedural details, and medication parameters, were collected for all participants. Important variables were selected using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression in the training set. We developed extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), random forest, decision tree, and logistic regression (LR) models and evaluated their discrimination, calibration, and classification metrics in the hold-out test set and external cohort. Results: In the training set, we identified 6 important variables (Killip class, lactate, estimated glomerular filtration rate, use of diuretics, use of beta-blockers, and use of renin-angiotensin system inhibitors). In the test set, model discrimination was comparable across XGBoost (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] 0.882, 95% CI 0.816-0.947), LR (AUC 0.875, 95% CI 0.799-0.950), and random forest (AUC 0.870, 95% CI 0.800-0.940), while decision tree showed lower performance (AUC 0.814, 95% CI 0.720-0.886). Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) values illustrated both global and individual feature contributions in the XGBoost model. A nomogram based on LR achieved an AUC of 0.873 (95% CI 0.714-0.926) in external validation. Conclusions: Our study identified 6 important predictors and provided a series of prediction models to enhance risk stratification of MARCE for patients with AMI and CKD. These models might aid in stratifying risk and choosing appropriate therapeutic strategies in the management of patients with AMI and CKD.
title: Explainable Machine Learning for Predicting Major Adverse Renal and Cardiovascular Events in Acute Myocardial Infarction With Chronic Kidney Disease: Algorithm Development and Validation

summary: In a cross-sectional analysis of traditional Medicare Fee-For-Service beneficiaries aged 66 years or older with outpatient oncology-related encounters, we found that telehealth modestly extended patient-provider geographic reach but largely operated within existing office-based catchments and preserved rural-urban distance gradients. Equitable telehealth policy should target patients with high travel burden while supporting digital access, navigation, and cross-jurisdiction continuity.
title: Patient-Provider Distance in Medicare Outpatient Oncology Telehealth Versus Office Visits, 2021‐2023: Cross-Sectional Claims Analysis

summary: Background: Cough variant asthma (CVA) is a prevalent but underdiagnosed subtype of chronic cough, largely due to the limited accessibility of pulmonary function tests in primary care. Objective: This study aimed to develop and prospectively validate an interpretable machine learning model using routine laboratory data to facilitate accessible CVA screening. Methods: We conducted a multicenter study combining retrospective model development and prospective validation using data from January 2021 to August 2025. The study included 3 sets—a retrospective development set (n=533; 428 training and 105 internal testing) and 2 prospective validation sets (internal validation: n=59 and external validation: n=78). In total, 54 routine biochemical, coagulation, and hematological markers were analyzed. A Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN) model was developed and benchmarked against extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost). Performance was evaluated via area under the curve (AUC), accuracy, and specificity. Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) and decision curve analysis (DCA) were used to assess interpretability and clinical utility. Results: In external validation, TabPFN achieved an AUC of 0.858 (95% CI 0.763-0.943), accuracy of 79.5%, sensitivity of 71.4%, and specificity of 86%. XGBoost achieved a higher external AUC of 0.912 (95% CI 0.842-0.982) and sensitivity of 91.4%, but lower accuracy (75.6%) and specificity (62.8%) at the fixed 0.5 probability threshold. TabPFN retained higher AUCs than XGBoost in internal testing (0.964 vs 0.890) and temporal validation (0.925 vs 0.846). DCA demonstrated that TabPFN provided higher net benefit across clinically relevant threshold probabilities, with the range varying across validation cohorts. SHAP analysis identified serum sodium (Na) and prothrombin time international normalized ratio as the leading predictors, followed jointly by mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration and red cell distribution width-SD, which showed the same rounded mean absolute SHAP value at the reported 2-decimal precision, and elevated sodium levels (>141 mmol/L) were associated with increased predicted risk. Conclusions: The TabPFN model demonstrated robust prospective performance as an accessible screening tool for CVA, with balanced threshold-dependent classification performance across validation cohorts. Although TabPFN showed higher discrimination than XGBoost in internal and temporal validation, XGBoost achieved a higher AUC in the external cohort, indicating that neither model uniformly outperformed the other across all performance dimensions.
title: Screening for Cough Variant Asthma Using the TabPFN Model on Routine Laboratory Data in a Multicenter Cohort: Prospective Validation Study
